what_it_does: When two large sparse matrices (matrices where most entries are zero) are multiplied together, a common hardware approach feeds one row of the first matrix at a time into the chip and looks up matching rows in the second matrix. The problem is that adjacent rows often access completely different parts of the second matrix, so the chip must fetch the same data from off-chip memory repeatedly. Bootes reorders the rows of the first matrix before the multiplication starts, using a math technique called spectral clustering (which groups rows by how similar their non-zero patterns are) so that nearby rows share more data lookups and memory traffic drops. A small decision-tree classifier first checks whether reordering will actually help for a given matrix — skipping it when it would waste time — and the reordering itself is made 11x faster than prior approaches, keeping the preprocessing cost manageable.
